doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Tape splicing and editing as a second engineer
summary: Hank recalls being nervous about splicing, working as second engineer at Capitol on Peggy Lee and Sinatra dates, and demanding quiet while editing.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: The first time I ever saw in the studio tape slicing and splicing I was amazed that it worked. I just didn’t know such a thing was done the first time I saw it. So do you recall the first time you ever did that and were you nervous about it?

You bet. But it didn’t happen very often. If I was a second engineer working behind let’s say John Krause at Capitol — I mean he would — in those days on a date, I’m talking about twenty years ago, the engineer could turn around and say, “Would you take the first half of the tune up through the first chorus and cut it to the next take of the same chorus.” You know and that happens on a date, when there’s twenty guys in the room talking. That’s when you can get in trouble, I mean as a second engineer. I as an engineer would get into a situation like that sometimes because the producers would like, “I’d like to hear the first chorus I loved in the tune, the bridge I loved that, but could you give me the second chorus of take twelve.” Then you’ve got to juggle and whizzle around. And hopefully you can make all the cuts.
Am I correct that you would manipulate the tape over the heads so that you would hear —

Absolu— yes. No, I’ll tell you what, you want pressure? You’re working on a — at Capitol, I’m working on a Peggy Lee date or something. And as a second engineer you’re running the machines. And then the producer says, “But could we keep the first chorus on that take and go to take twelve” or whatever, “and put that second chorus together.” And usually it’s the second engineer who is running the machines that does the editing if he’s good. And I mean if you’re working at Capitol or Columbia they expect those second engineers to be able to do that and inevitably — let’s say you’re working on a Sinatra date, which I did many times, and he’d say, “Take the first chorus from this take and put that together.” And they come in the control room and they’re all talking. And you’re trying to make an edit. And I would say “Shut the F up I can’t hear what I’m doing.” “Oh okay.” “Take it outside I can’t hear what I’m doing.” I mean you make an edit and if you © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
make a dumb edit and you screw it up you look like a fool. Don’t look like a fool, tell them to get the hell out of the room so you can hear what you are doing.
